strengths: The problem has an identifiable audience in Bayesian optimization and Pareto active learning: identifying an approximately correct Pareto set over continuous design spaces with controlled evaluation costs.

The algorithm offers a coherent combination of regional confidence rectangles, inherited uncertainty bounds, and adaptive refinement. Distinguishing uncertainty from observations and variation within cells is useful.
The high-level exposition, algorithm diagrams, and extensive appendix make the intended method and proof strategy accessible.

The experiments include ten GP function draws, five repetitions per function, four baselines, and explicit runtime measurements. The tree-depth comparison usefully exposes the difference between sample efficiency and computational efficiency.
weaknesses: Required: repair the proof supporting Theorem 1. In Corollary 1, the chosen u contains h log N, so Lemma 7's 2u contributes 2h log N, whereas the stated V_h contains only h log N. The simultaneous confidence event therefore does not follow from the displayed calculation. In Lemma 14, equation (31) applies the parent's refinement condition using the current confidence multiplier, although that condition held at an earlier time and β increases. An argument using the inherited rectangle at refinement time could address the latter issue, but the stated guarantees need a corrected derivation.

Required: correct or remove Proposition 1 and its claimed demonstration that the dimension bound can outperform the information bound. Appendix C obtains a lower bound proportional to T times a coefficient involving a_Tj²/(a_Tj²+σ²); this coefficient depends on T and need not remain positive uniformly. Keeping the independent bump amplitudes bounded away from zero instead creates infinitely many uniformly separated points in the GP metric, incompatible with compactness and Assumption 1. The assertion that a suitable metric exists does not resolve this problem.

Required: reconcile the experimental metrics with Definitions 3–5. Section 7.1 tests accuracy by asking whether a predicted point is ε-dominated by a true Pareto point. An arbitrarily inferior point satisfies that test, although it should be excluded from Z_ε. The stated equivalences between ε-domination and 2ε-domination are also incorrect. Specify the implemented inequalities and verify or recompute the results accordingly. Report accuracy and coverage separately; their average in Table 2 cannot substantiate the probability of returning an entirely valid ε-accurate set.

Required: qualify the practical efficiency claims. The theoretical-depth setting takes 15:15:24, whereas the fast settings replace V_h by zero at a finite depth. Zero does not bound variation over positive-width cells, so these implementations do not inherit the continuous-region guarantee as presented. Clearly distinguish their empirical performance from the certified algorithm. The broad superiority claims should also be narrowed to the tested one-dimensional, independent-objective GP setting unless additional evidence is supplied.

Required for implementation and interpretation: Algorithm 1 computes the pessimistic Pareto set before constructing the current rectangles on which it depends. The root also needs explicit conventions because V_0 contains log(0) and its confidence bounds reference a nonexistent parent. Finally, explain how the returned union of cells becomes the finite prediction set used in experiments and how comparable recommendations are extracted from each baseline.

Optional after correcting and narrowing the claims: correlated-objective and higher-dimensional experiments, together with a controlled comparison against uniform discretization, would help establish when adaptation offers practical benefits. These extensions are not prerequisites for a sound, clearly delimited theoretical contribution.
